title: Interpretability Across the Activation Spectrum
takeaway: Scoring each band of a unit's activation range separately, the paper's human annotator judged strong activations far more consistent with a feature's interpretation than weak ones. Autoencoder features average above the annotator's interpretability threshold only from roughly the 20% band upward, while MLP neurons stay far below it everywhere. So the monosemanticity claim is strongest exactly where features fire hardest, and thinnest at the bottom of the spectrum.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

This is a result from the blinded [[manual-interpretability-scoring]] run, cut up by activation strength rather than reported as one number per unit.

Each scored sample is an [[activation-interval]]: one of eleven evenly spaced bands between zero and that unit's own maximum activation. The annotator sampled examples uniformly from every band, so weak firings got looked at as often as strong ones. That design is the correction for [[max-dataset-example-bias]] — judging a unit only by its hardest firings, which can make a [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] unit look clean.

### How to read it

The x axis is the band, labelled as a fraction of the unit's maximum: `~0%` is the weakest band, `~100%` the strongest. It is relative, not absolute — each unit is normalised to its own peak.

The y axis is one line item of the [[feature-interpretability-rubric]], scored 0–5. The annotator first commits to a single interpretation of the whole unit. Then, band by band, they rate how consistent that band's high-activating tokens are with that one interpretation.

So a low score here does not mean "this band is confusing on its own". It means this band disagrees with the story the rest of the unit tells.

The dotted line at 3 is the authors' own subjective threshold for calling something interpretable. It is a judgement call, not a derived cutoff.

Two series are drawn. Magenta is [[feature|features]] from the [[sparse-autoencoder]]; teal is the raw MLP neurons of the same model, scored identically as the baseline. The faded dots sit at integer scores, darker where more intervals landed there; the lines are per-band averages.

### What it shows

Both curves climb left to right. Features start around 2.6 in the weakest band, cross the threshold near the 20% band, reach about 4.3 by 40%, and sit between 4.3 and 4.8 above that.

Neurons rise too — about 0.3 to about 1.9 — but never approach 3. The dark teal dot at 0 in every column is the usual neuron outcome: no hypothesis fits at all.

The rise is what matters. The paper offers no confident account of the low end, suggesting only that a learned direction sitting [[feature-at-slight-angle|at a slight angle]] to the true one would misbehave there.

That is the soft spot, and the paper says so: most real activations are small, so [[low-interval-activation-skew|most activations fall in the worst-scoring bands]]. Its defence is that [[large-activations-dominate|large activations carry most of the effect]] on the model's output.

terms.term: Manual Evaluation by Activation Interval (chart title)
terms.definition: Names the experiment: the blinded human interpretability scoring, broken out by how strongly the unit was firing on the examples being judged, rather than aggregated into one score per unit.
Which band of the unit's activation range the scored examples were drawn from. It is a position within a unit's own range, not an activation magnitude comparable across units.

The eleven activation intervals, each labelled by the fraction of that unit's maximum activation it sits at. The tildes mark them as approximate bins: examples nearest that fraction, not examples at exactly it.
The score the human annotator assigned to that band, on the paper's own scoring scheme for how interpretable a unit is. Only one item of that scheme is plotted here, not the full total.

The specific rubric item being plotted: how consistent that interval's high-activating tokens are with the interpretation the annotator formed from the unit's whole activation spectrum. It measures agreement with a fixed hypothesis, not standalone clarity.
Directions learned by the sparse autoencoder trained on the one-layer transformer's MLP activations. These are the candidate units of interpretation the paper is arguing for.
The individual MLP neurons of the same transformer, scored on the same rubric by the same annotator. They are the baseline the features are meant to beat.

The score at or above which the authors say they subjectively considered an interval interpretable. The label's own word 'subjective' flags it as the annotator's impression rather than a measured cutoff.

The individual scored intervals, drawn at each whole-number score for each band, with opacity standing in for how many intervals landed there. Where a magenta and a teal dot coincide the colours blend to grey.
The average interval-consistency score across all scored intervals in that band, one line per series. They are means over a small sample, so single-band wobbles should not be read as signal.
The full range of values a unit takes across the dataset, from just above zero up to its maximum. The paper's argument is that a unit must be checked across all of it, not only at the top.
The scorer (one of the authors) did not know whether a given unit was an autoencoder feature or a raw neuron while scoring it, which is what makes the two series comparable.

numbers.meaning: The number of activation intervals, hence the number of x positions. The range from zero to a unit's maximum activation is cut into evenly spaced bands, and examples are sampled uniformly from each so the whole spectrum gets equal attention.

The range of the plotted rubric item. The full rubric runs 0–14 across five items; interval consistency is the single 0–5 item asking how well a band's strongly-firing tokens match the annotator's interpretation.
The height of the dotted threshold line. The paper says it subjectively regarded features as interpretable above this score; it is stated as a judgement, with no calibration behind it.
The feature average in the weakest band (~0%). Below the threshold: at the bottom of the spectrum, a feature's firings often do not match the story the rest of its spectrum tells.
The band where the feature line crosses the threshold of 3. Everything to the left is, by the paper's own cutoff, not interpretable on average.
The feature average at the ~40% band, and also the dip at ~80%. The jump between the ~30% and ~40% bands is the sharpest step in the curve.
The highest feature averages, at the ~70% and ~100% bands. Near the ceiling of 5, meaning nearly every strongly-firing example agreed with the interpretation.
The neuron average across the range, weakest band to strongest. Neurons improve with activation strength on the same trend as features, but never come near the threshold of 3.

The score at which the darkest teal dot sits in every column. The paper reports that the median neuron scored 0 on the full rubric, meaning the annotator could not form any hypothesis about it at all.

The point the text gives for a pattern behind the averages: some features stay consistent across roughly the top 60% of their spectrum and then fall off quickly below it. Others are consistent all the way down.
The total number of activation intervals scored, which is the population the dots and averages are drawn from. Roughly 37 per band if evenly split, so each average rests on a small sample.
The number of features and neurons those intervals came from. Manual scoring is slow, which is why the sample is this small.

Reported elsewhere in the same section, not on this chart: the median feature interval's total rubric score out of 14 versus the median neuron's. Given for scale on how far apart the two series are on the full rubric.
